Oral History - Kenny Clarke
Sides 1-4

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.

P R O C E E D I N G S
Okay. We're talking to Kenny Clarke.
Maybe I (Unintelligible).
Yeah, be comfortable. We'll try it, because I can easily pick it up, and we'll just try this like this.
Okay.

So we're talking to Kenny Clarke. It's the 30th of September, 1977. Helen Oakley Dance (UNINTELLIGIBLE), and in Paris, and Kenny's going to do the interview now. Now we're going to see what kind of a shot we've got on that. Okay, Kenny. Just let me get a little shot on your voice.
Okay, Helen. I think this is a very nice thing, and I think we should get some very nice things done.
Good enough. Okay. Well, Kenny, what we want to do is go right back to the beginning.
(Laughter)
We want to know about your family, where the musical elements came from and everything.
Well, Helen, I was born in Pittsburgh, exactly 63 years ago, and my mother was a very good pianist and she began teaching me to dance and to play the piano. She

would put me on her knee and we would play for hours and just different songs. I imagine I was about five and a half years old. And I created -- developed a love for the piano, unbelievable. And I played piano, sadly to say (Unintelligible), until my mother died, and then I was completely -- I had forgotten about music. I forgot about music completely.
Well, how old -- what happened?
Well, after momma died --
How old were you when your momma died?
Well, I was about six and a half years old.
Oh.
And I was just beginning to really understand the piano and rhythms and chord changes and things like that.
You might have been a piano player.
I'm sure I would have. That's sure. I have no doubt about that.
What a shame.
And I just gave up music altogether until I guess they put me away in a place, sort of a boarding school.
Well, listen. Tell me why. Did you have brothers and sisters?
Yes, an older brother. He was two years
Did you go together?
Yes, we did.
Because there wasn't anyone to take care of you.
No. My father left. I don't know. And there we were, two boys......
Oh.

With no mother. So an uncle put us away in a place called the Coleman Industrial Home, where there were some excellent musicians. I was really -- I couldn't believe it. And the teacher, Mr. Moore, he was capable of playing all the instruments. And then I became interested in music again because I loved him so much.
Well, how wonderful. What age did you become interested again?
Oh, about eight.
Oh, as early as that.
As early as that. We -- well, they had a marching band there.
Yeah.
And Mr. Moore knew of my musical background. He knew that I could solfegge. He knew that I could read a little bit. So then he started me to playing the alto horn, the peck horn as we called it.
The brass horn.
Yeah. And from there I went to the baritone horn and then the trumpet, and the trombone, until, well, the brass instruments just didn't appeal to me like I thought they would.
NO.

And he says, 'Well, Kenny, why don't you try the drums, why don't you try to play marches.' So he taught me the drums. You know, the snare drums. And I began to play, to march and play with the band. And then I guess -- I imagine I was about 11, and then there was a completely hiatus. I just -- I don't know what happened. I just seemed to have forgot about music entirely until I was about 17. Just completely faded away after I left there. My stepfather took me away from there.
When you were 11.
When I was about 11.
Oh.
And it just cut me off from music. And with him there was no music. There was no friends who played music and I was just sort of isolated.
Well, Kenny, now wait a minute. Now you said your stepfather.
Uh-huh.
Well, when your momma died your
stepfather was at home, but your father --
No, my father, he went to Yakima, Washington, to raise apples for a great aunt.
Your father did?
Uh-huh.
Really?
Uh-huh.
What, out on the West Coast, you mean?
Yes, on the West Coast, in Yakima.
Oh.
And my great aunt had quite a bit of property out there and they raised apples, and that's where he --
And that's where your father had gone.
That's where my father had gone.
Yeah. And then, so when your mom died, your stepfather just didn't know what to -- how to cope.
That's right. He had no idea --
What to do.
-- what our family was all about in the first place.
No. No. I see.
so --
But then it was your stepfather who five years later came and got you out?
Yeah, got me out.
Well, what about your brother?
Well, both of us.
What's your brother's name?
Charles.
Oh.
He took both of us out and --
That was decent, wasn't it?
Yes, I thought it was very nice of him.
Was he married then?
No, no. He was alone.
All alone and he took you?
And he took us. He couldn't stand the idea that we were away from him, because I guess he'd been with us, oh, since I was about three or four.
Is that so.
And he became attached to us and he kept us until his death.
Did he really.
Uh-huh.
What did he do?
Well, he was a preacher.
Oh.
A very --
What, a sanctified preacher or a Baptist church, or what?
A Baptist church. He was a very educated
man. And I learned a lot from him. But as far as music was concerned, he had little interest in it, outside of the choir and things like that.
Yeah.
And we had an apartment in the church and we lived there.
Fancy that. That's amazing, really, isn't it?
And, well --
So what did you do, which school did you go to there?

I went to the Washington School with a lot of Jewish kids, and one of them is a friend of mine today. He's an impresario here in Paris, and we went to school, when we were about 12 or 13 years old, together.
How strange. What's his name?
Isn't that? Bernard Hildq. Have you ever heard of Bernard Hildq?
I think the name's familiar to me. Whom does he handle?
Oh, lots of acts. I don't remember now.
Oh, well, it doesn't matter. I just thought I'd ask.
But he had an orchestra at the time, and when I came to Paris with Dizzy and I stayed over and he

asked me to play with him. Now, we didn't recognize each other that time, because this was like '40, almost 30 years. So we began talking one day and he said, 'Little Kenny. Pittsburgh.' He said, 'I know a little Kenny from Pittsburgh, used to go to Washington School.' I said, 'Well, that's me.' He said, 'It can't be true.' And we found that we had been kids together.
: Isn't that funny. That is really very funny isn't it.
But he was a violinist, a very good violinist, who loved Rubinoff at the time. You know, he was a great fan of Rubinoff.
: Yeah.
And I became attached to him because there was music, you know?
: Yeah. Was your brother --
My brother, no, he wasn't interested in music until I started playing the drums.
: Then did he --
Then he wanted to play the drums too. He was a very good drummer, a very good drummer.
: Why do you say was?
Huh?
: Why do you say was?
Well, he's dead now. He died about two
months ago. : Oh, Kenny, where, at home?
Yeah, in Pittsburgh.
: Oh.
About two months ago.
: Was he a musician then?
He was a musician in his --
: In his heart.
-- heart. He was a strong musician.
But what happened, I had an uncle, John Buchanan Booz his name was. He was --
: How do you spell that?
B-o-o-z.
: Yeah.
Like booze, without the e.
: Without the e, yeah.
And he was an exceptionally good surgeon.
: I see.
And he loved my brother so much, he sent him to West Virginia State to study. Willy had a 'horse', as we called it, you know, a scholarship, because he was a very good basketball player, so they --
: Was he tall?
Well, quite, yeah. My father was like six, three.
Fancy that.
I'm the runt. They all call me the runt.
(Laughter)
I was the smallest one in the family.
Did you take after your mother?
Yes, I thought so. Yeah. Very much.
Yeah.
But all my sisters -- well my father married again while he was in Yakima, and I have something like seven brothers and sisters, and they're all giants.
How funny. How funny. Nobody believes you when you say that.
They baby me when I see them. But --
So he sent your brother to study what, medicine?
To study medicine at the West Virginia State, which he had a scholarship on account of him being the basketball coach.
Yeah.

So, well, he had been in school a couple of years, and then all of a sudden we didn't hear from him. So Uncle John says, 'Kenny, it's strange I haven't heard from Charles for about six months. What's going on?' You know, he was so busy running and delivering babies and operating and this and that, so he sort of left it up to me to keep contact with

Well, I couldn't. You know, I couldn't get word to him. So he said, 'Okay, we'll drive down one Sunday and see exactly what's going on.' So we arrived at the university and we asked around, and they said, 'Oh, Charles. Well, he left school about three months ago.' So my Uncle John said, 'Oh, no, this is impossible.' So the director, he said, 'Well, listen, there's a man came here from Clarksburg, West Virginia, and he left with him.' So we said, well, let's go to Clarksburg. So he went to Clarksburg and found this family, the Winston family, and they said that Charles was in Weirton, West Virginia. Weirton. So Uncle John said, 'What's going on?' So we went to Weirton and he was working in this steel mill, and we found out that --
Why did he do it?
Well, he made this little girl pregnant.
Yeah.
And the father came with a shotgun and obliged him to marry the girl and get a job, because he had to support her.
And he wouldn't tell Uncle John.
No, because Uncle John wouldn't support a girl, you know. So --
Oh, cut his medical career.
Yes, his whole medical career was shot.
Right from under his feet.
So --
What an awful shame.
He would have been a wonderful doctor, I know it.
What a shame.

So the thing that -- what happened, after I met the girl, she was such a beautiful person and so intelligent I couldn't believe it. And she was such a wonderful person, so I said, "Charles you couldn't have married a better person." Well, she turned out to be the head of the family.
Well, I'll be darned. Isn't that -- you never do quite know why things happen, do you.
No, things happen.
I mean he could have only been about what, 18, 19?

Oh, at that time, let's see, I was in Cincinnati with a band from Pittsburgh, Leroy Bradley's band, and we had been working for these Volpe brothers in Homestead. And we got this job to go to Cincinnati, at the Cotton Club, to be the house band. And I was 19, so Charles must have been at least 20, you know, 21. Because he only had five years more, which he would have had his doctor's degree about 28. So at that time he was about 22.
What a shame.
Isn't that something.
Terrible. So what did he go on and do?
Well, he took a job in the post office.
Got out of the steel mill student element.

The girl's father was keeping him. He was a very mean man. But her mother was a jewel, she was so sweet. But she said, 'Sam is so mean. I hope Charles obeys him, because I wouldn't want him to hurt Charles.'
Gosh.
So what happened really, after they moved to Pittsburgh and -- from West Virginia they moved to Pittsburgh.
Yeah.
And --
So he got away from the father.

And I was in Cincinnati, so I asked Charles, I said, 'Come out here with me and get your mind together, because out here you can just lay down and rest and listen to music and probably change your whole scheme of things.'
Yeah.
So he says okay, so he came out.
What, he and his wife?
No, just him. He came alone.
To think everything out.
Yeah, to think everything out for himself.
Yeah.

And talk with me. So, well, he stayed there about a couple of weeks, and then he became homesick. He said, 'I want to go back and see what Evelyn is doing. I'm kind of worried. Evelyn and the baby are alone.' So he went back to Pittsburgh, and I stayed in Cincinnati, oh, quite a while, I stayed out there about six months. And Andy Kirk's band --
I've got to stop you. We've got to go back, because we got onto your brother but we left you at the age of 14 --
Yeah.
-- at school.
Right.
And this is important. We've got to find out how this happened. So all right, back you go.
Okay. Well, you see, I was going --
Oh, yeah, you met the friend, the fellow that's the agent here.
Yeah, Bernard Hilda.
Bernard Hilda.
Yeah. Well, his people moved to Paris, you know, as soon as he finished secondary school.
Really?
His family moved to Paris, because I think his father became an ambassador or something. They were
French anyway, but his father married --
How do you spell that name, H-i-l-d-a?
Yeah, that's right.
Hilda.
Bernard Hilda.
I do think I've heard the name, yeah.
He's a very famous band leader.
Yeah.
So his father was an ambassador, was a French citizen, though, he had something to do with politics. And they went back -- his father moved back to France and took the family.
So how old was Bernard at that time, would you say?
Oh, Bernard was about 15.
Yeah.
Uh-huh. So then I went on to -- we were living in the same neighborhood. I went on to another school, something like in our neighborhood, but I had left secondary and went to high school.
What was it called?
Herron Hill High School.
Oh, I was just wondering if I'll hear another familiar name of Earl's, but I don't remember that one, no.
Well, Herron Hill High School and the Schenley High School, are the two famous schools.
Well, I think he did say that.
Schenley High.
Yeah.
Uh-huh.
That's where he went.
So after graduation from high school --
Well, but had you started playing drums then?
No, not really. You know, just fooling around professionally.
You'd go and listen to Bernard, but you'd --
You know, yeah, just listen to him, but I'd never played anything, you know.
No. And you didn't have your instrument.

No. I hadn't chosen my instrument, really. I wanted to play the piano, but the piano lessons were so expensive and we didn't have much money, so I knew my stepfather would never consent to giving me piano lessons, because he didn't understand, you know.
That's right. He had no feel for the [piano.]
He thought it would just be throwing away money.
Sure.
So anyway, I thought that maybe if I played the church organ, maybe he would --
That's right.
So I did start playing it, but that still didn't convince him.
But did you know enough to play a church organ?
Oh, yes, I could play. My mother taught me all these things, and I remembered everything.
At six?
I remembered --
All those chords?
"Nearer My God to Thee," all the --
Fancy that.
"Just a Little Walk with Thee." I knew all those songs.
So you couldn't read, but you knew them.
I knew those songs by ear, you know.
Fancy that. But isn't it hard to play the organ? Were you using --
No, it was a pump organ. You know, a pump organ in church.
Well, doesn't it have levels?
Yes, it has a two keyboard, a double keyboard.
Two keyboard. And you could do that?
Uh-huh. Yeah, I could play that thing.
Fancy that.
Yes. I could play it in church.
Fancy that.
All the church songs, you know, I could play.
That must have pleased him all the same.
Yeah, he was very happy that I could play, you know.
Yeah.
But he never thought, it never dawned on him, that you know, --
That you could go further with that.

No, I guess people at that time, they were very backward, to an extent, a certain portion of the people were, were very backward. They were thinking about oh, Lord, this, and they were very religious and that's as far as it got.
Horizons were small.
Uh-huh. Right. They never entered into,
really, the modern world.
No.
They just stayed, you know.
Yeah.
So when I finished school I just left home.
Yeah.
You know, I was just so disgusted.
Yeah.

And I met -- which I was just about 17, you know. I didn't have a job or anything. So there was a friend of mine in school named Frank Clarke who was a wonderful bassist, you know, and well we had a band at Herron Hill, so we had a -- oh, what's his name? He was an Irish fellow. He taught Ray Brown and all those bass players from Pittsburgh.
Really? Well, does Ray Brown come from Pittsburgh?
Yes, uh-huh.
Oh, I didn't realize that.
What was his name? I should never forget his name.
No kidding.
And he was an Irish fellow, but he could play all of the instruments, and he began to let us take instruments home, and then we formed a little band, you know, in
Did he have a little money, that he owned these different instruments?
No, he would requisition them from the school. And tell us to be careful and so forth, and don't break the instruments, and -- oh, if I could just think of his name.
Well, it'll come to you. Maybe overnight it'll come to you.
It'll come to me.
And you can tell me tomorrow. We'll put it on. Fancy that. So what did you take home?
Well, I took the snare drum home.
Yeah.
You know?
Yeah.

And another friend of mine, Eugene, he began to really play snare drum very well, and like he lived close to me so we would always be together and he would show me things that I didn't understand. And so from that, after I left school, there was a friend of mine who was a dancer, and he asked -- he invited me, 'Come up to the club where we're dancing, and I would like you to see, you know, understand the different rhythms and things.'
Oh, yes.
So I said, 'Oh, I think that would be very interesting.'
How nice.
So we went to the club.
What was his name?
John Porcher his name was, P-o-r-c-h-e-r.
Oh, he was also French background or something, wasn't he?
Yes, he was.
Sounds like it.
Uh-huh. Because I know some Porchers here.
Yeah.
And I often think of Johnny. He was a wonderful dancer.
About the same age as you?

Yeah, the same age, and a marvelous dancer. So I used to hang out with him a lot because he hung around musical people and dancers and singers, you know, in show business, which I was never introduced to show business before, and I thought it was something incredible. I never saw all these wonderful people singing and dancing. That just struck me. I said, 'Oh, God, this is where I want to be.'
Yeah.
So the drummer was going home to visit his
mother in Newport -- no, Newport News, Virginia.
Oh, yeah.
And it was --
The A fort or something,
wasn't it?
Yeah.
Yeah.
And he said, 'Kenny, do you think you can play till I get back?
can play till I get back?
Oh, he actually had a job?
Yeah, he was working, and that's where all these show people would hang out.
Oh.
So I said -- his name was Biddy Johnson.
Biddy?
Biddy Johnson.
B-i-d-d-y.
Uh-uh. B-i-d-d-i-e.
-- i-e, yeah.

And he says, 'Do you think you could hold the job down? I'll just be gone a couple of weeks.' So I said, 'Listen, Biddie, I'm afraid --,' He said, 'Oh, think nothing of it. I'll be here a couple of days and you come every night and I'll show you just how it goes.
But you had to play for dancers.
Uh-huh. So we had a wonderful saxophone player named Gene Jenkins.
Oh? G-e-n-e?
Yeah. Who just said, "Kenny, you come and don't you worry about anything. I'll take care of you."
That's nice.
Oh, my God. So Biddie went away and I began to work there. Oh, the first night I was scared out of my mind and out of my wits. I didn't know what to do.
Well, how many guys -- who was in -- how many guys were in the band?
Well, we only had three. The pianist, the saxophonist --
And you.
-- and drums.
Yeah. No-one to keep the beat going but a lead over you.
Oh, I was scared out of my wits.
Yeah.

I didn't know what to do. So first night, Gene said, "Don't worry. Everything is okay. I'll take care of you." So, oh, about a week, then I got the swing of things, with the help of Gene. Everything came just so easily, because he was so patient and such a wonderful person.
And you had that natural feeling for it.
That's right. So about a week, I was
playing for the dances and Johnny was encouraging me and everything, and I said, "Oh, my God, I'm in."
You were what, about 17?
Yeah, about 17.
Yeah.
So I stayed there and worked awhile. Then the musicians got word, "Oh, there's a new drummer around, a young kid. Oh, he sure plays well." So that was the beginning.
It started already, did it, right away?
Yeah, it started right away.
Fancy that.
So then the fellow --
Because I mean they weren't really mad about your friend, but when you got in there they did.
Yes, they did.
How about that.
So a bandleader from -- where was he from? From the North Side, a wonderful pianist. He was really --
What's his name?

George Hornsby. So he had an orchestra and he said -- he came in the club one night and he said, "Hey, kid, can you read?" I said, "Well, I can make out," you know. So he said, "Well, let me hear something fast." So Gene, who

would always take care of me, you know, he would play something, so he said, "That's pretty good. Here's my address and everything and here's where we rehearse. Now, do you think you could be there tomorrow about 2:00 o'clock?" So I said, "Well, I'll try, you know." So he said, "Well, don't worry about an instrument, because our trumpet player, he's an instrument repair man, so we have all the instruments that we need." So I said okay, and the next day I went, and they had a lot of stock arrangements which were very simple to read, and he said --
Well, could you actually read anything?
Yes, I could read.
Who had taught you that?
Mama taught me how to --
The notes?
The difference in --
The beat, the time.
The rhythm and time, you know, different quarter notes and eighth rests and all that.
No kidding.
Yeah, I knew all that.
Fancy that.
And I began to play with them and he said, "Gee, kid, you're nice." And I stayed with a big band. I guess we were about 14 pieces. And that did it.
And everybody was much older than you.
Oh, yes. And that did it for me. And then Roy Eldridge heard me.
What, way back then?
Oh, yeah. I was with Roy Eldridge in 1932.
Well, listen, let's see, we didn't actually say what year this was when you were 17. You were born in 1914.
Because I remember the next year I went with Roy, that Roosevelt -- that Prohibition was repealed, and we were working in nightclubs at that time, and when beer came in then --
Well, listen, what about the union?
Well, the union wasn't very --
[End of Side 1]
So go on about that.
So I gigged around with George Hornsby for quite awhile, and then something strange happened to George. He became religious and he joined the church and began to play just church music.
Was he a white boy?
No, he was a colored boy. After He'd written so many beautiful things.
Songs, even?
Yes, he just turned right around and went religious, and he started playing in the churches. So then I left George --
Did he ever end up doing anything?
Not really. He just stayed in the church all the time. He never came out.
Did he become a preacher?
No, just a musician in -- he wanted to be close to the church.
Fancy that.
Can you imagine?
It's unusual.
And A wonderful pianist.
Fancy that.
And he had written many good songs that Fletcher Henderson played.
Which ones, do you remember?
Oh. I think Hawk took one of his tunes.
Oh, not, 'Hello, Lola,' or, 'One Hour.'
No, it was something like, 'Changes,' or
something, it was called.
Oh. And made it with the band?
Yeah, just went through the keys.
Not, 'Queer Notions.' Because 'Queer Notions' went through a heck of a lot of changes.
That could have been it, because --
Oh, did he write a number like that?
Very modern chords.
Yes. That was around -- that was about '32.
Fancy that. That'd be the right time.
Uh-huh. And that's the year I joined Roy, and --
Well tell me, first of all, when did you and Roy first meet? Which school did Roy go to?
Well, Roy went to school on the north side.
What was the name of his school?
I don't know, really.
Oh. Was he the same age as you?
Roy? No, he was a little older, and he had an older brother.
Joe.
Joe, yeah.
Yeah.
Who really was really an extraordinary musician as far -- he was a good teacher.
An alto player.
Yes, he was an alto player and arranger.
Joe died, didn't he?
Yes. Well, I was in his funeral the last time I was home.
When?

This was -- well, let's see, I went home -- let me get it straight now. When was I home? Let's see, Joe died about -- I went out to the hospital to see him. We decided to all go out to the hospital, and when we arrived at the hospital I went up to the desk and then she said, 'Don't you know? Mr. Eldridge passed away about two hours ago.' I said, 'Well, I couldn't know, because my trip was about an hour.'
Oh, how awful.
Let's see.
Imagine that. Roy wasn't there.
Yeah, Roy was there.
You and Roy went out? Oh, he was --
Yeah, when I was home, see?
Yeah. Roy was there at --
Let's see. I'll tell you exactly when. Was it -- it was right after I came out of the army. This must
have been 1946 or '47. Oh, for heaven's sake.
And so we all went to Joe's funeral and everything.
That was sad, wasn't it.
Oh, it was very. He was really something. For me he was really --
Was he? He was very schooled, wasn't he?
Yes, very. And he --
And he wrote.
Oh, very well. Very well. Wonderful arranger. And I joined the band, we were playing in a cabaret in Pittsburgh.
Now what year are you in?
Now I'm in around '32.
Oh. So -- you are in '32. Had you ever heard Roy blow?
Oh, yeah. He used to jam. I used to hear him jamming in all the clubs around home.
Well, what clubs did you used to go to to jam?
Well, let me see, there was The Brown Derby.
Yeah.
There was a fellow, Gus Greenlee's club. What was the name of that club?
Oh, it doesn't matter, Kenny.
But we had quite a few clubs around home at that time.
It was jumping.
Oh, yeah. Pittsburgh was the town.
Yeah.
And --
Lots of people didn't know that.

Oh, boy. Any musician, they were kind of afraid to come to Pittsburgh, because they could find their -- meet their match there, you know. I don't care what instrument you played, we were always running around and knock on the door of some trumpet player. And Little Louis, we used to call him, say, "Hey, Little Louis, there's a trumpet player from Fletcher Henderson's band who thinks he can blow." And Louis said, "Oh, yeah?" And he would take his horn right out, no case or nothing, just take his horn and run down to the cabaret and listen, and then start blowing.
Would he really blow?
Oh, Lord.
What was his last name?
I don't know. I don't remember what Louis's name was. We used to call him Little Louis. Yeah, he
was the one we would always get when we had a tough trumpet player from New York or somewhere. We'd call Louis and sometimes Roy would take over, you know.

Well, Roy didn't have all that, because when I knew Roy, which was, say, two years later -- I mean when Roy went into the Three Deuces, he explained to me then that he wasn't going to be able to blow anything for some months, because he was switching his embouchure armature so he could get range.
I see.

They hugged him and took him in the kitchen and I didn't see him for about three hours. The Japanese kept him in the kitchen all the time, feeding him and -- because they hadn't heard from home in years.
But Kenny, what -- the other guy stayed?
Yeah.
He settled down there?
He settled down there and they put him in a concentration camp after the attack on Pearl Harbor. And
he died in the concentration camp. Oh, they rounded up all the Americans, you know, and put them away like they did the Japanese here -- you know, the Japanese in --
Yeah, they made them labor and everything.
In California, yeah. He just couldn't take it, so -- Jimmy Brown, his name was. He died in -- so Carl and I, doing this --
Carl didn't want to go to Japan.
No, we decided to come to New York, because Ben Webster had told me, he says --
Well, you haven't told me -- oh, yeah. That's right. Because passing through Ben told you that.
Yeah, right. And he said, 'If you ever come to New York come to see me and don't worry about anything. I'll take care of you.'
Beautiful.
So it so happened that I had an aunt who was moving to New York.
What, your mother's sister?

Yeah. So I passed through Pittsburgh, and she said, 'Well, I'm going to New York, so I think the best thing for you two,' like Frank and I, 'is to come to New York if you're going to make it in music.' So I said okay. So she left about a month before we did. So Carl and I, we took a bus
out of Cincinnati and went to New York, with all these drums and the vibraphones wrapped in blankets.
(Laughter)
We came through the Holland Tunnel, and Call says, "Well, Kenny, here's New York." I said, "My God," and I started shaking. I was so afraid I didn't know what to do.
And you were only about 22?
Yes, about. Let's see, '36, yeah, I was 22.
Yeah.
Exactly 22.
This was '36.
Uh-huh. So as luck would have it --
So that's the very same year we when you came in the room started talking about, (Unintelligible).
Yeah, uh-huh. So what I did, Frank the bass player and I, and I was playing vibraphones, so we knew a good guitar player and we formed a trio.
Who was your guitar player?
Now, that's so far back --
(Laughter)
But we knew him from somewhere.
So wait a minute. So you had -- was Call playing piano?
Yeah, Carl was --
And there was you.
Myself --
And it was Frank.
Frank.
You didn't tell me Frank had come to New York.
Yeah, he came after I came.
Oh, I see.
He came after us.
Yeah.
And --
Did I ask you how to spell Frank's last name?
Yeah, Clarke? The same.
Oh, with an e?
Yeah.
Okay.
So we all -- it was a trio, a wonderful trio, it was Frank, Carl and myself. So we hired this guitar player, and --
Oh, I might even know, because Freddie took his place, huh?
No. No. This guitar player, he didn't make it very well. We were working for a guy in Harlem, he was
on 7th Avenue, he was a nice guy, he loved music, you know. And when I started playing the vibraphones, that did it. You know, he fell in love with the vibraphones. He loved the sound of it.
Well, where was this?
This was in Harlem.
Yeah, but what address?
This was around -- let's see, between -- between -- let me see, 122nd Street -- 122nd and 123rd Street.
Yeah.
This club was on the right hand side --
Of what?
Or the left hand side of 7th Avenue, going towards 110th Street.
I see.
And he had kind of a -- it wasn't quite a basement like, it was a step down.
Yeah.
You know how those private houses were.
Yeah, right. But you -- here you three guys -- or here you two guys arrive, and I mean no money, I presume.
No money.
So your aunt, where was she staying?
Well, she was staying on Lenox Avenue.
So did you move in with her?
Yeah, we moved in with her, so we were straight.
So what about food?
Oh, she was taking care of all that.
Oh, she was. So you didn't have to shake your own boots then.
No.
I mean you --
With the money we earned, you know, playing around --
You were lucky to start picking up change right away.
Oh, yeah, we were.
A lot of people just went hungry when they hit New York.
I know. Right after that -- now this is really strange -- Frank got a job, this job in the Black Cat, with Freddie Greene, you know, after our job ran out on 7th Avenue.
Yeah. Who was the piano player? Can you remember? Because Freddie was talking about him.
Fats Atkins.
Huh?
Fats Atkins. He was the first one that played like Basie.
Really?
Basie got his style -- because Basie played like J.P. Johnson.
Yeah.
But Basie got his style from Fats Atkins.
Now, that's funny Freddie didn't mention that.
Yeah.
Isn't that funny? I guess it just --
Fats Atkins used to (Imitating rhythm.)
Is that right?
That's where Basie got it. Let me show you how it happened.
Because somebody told me -- Jay McShann -- somebody the other day told us, said, that Basie used to sit down and they played two pianos -- I guess --
Uh-huh.
And Basie used to be playing up in the treble. So that's how come he developed that up there.
(Laughter)
The other guy was playing --
But he really --
No, it was Gene Hamey was telling me.
But Basie used to play tunes like,
"Prince Albert," and things like that, it was like J.P. Johnson.
Yeah.

But what happened -- and Basie, we've been tight for about 35 years. I used to just get on his bus and go everywhere. I don't care where -- I'd say, "Where you going, Base?" He'd say, "I'm going to so and so." Okay, I'm going too. I'd just get on the bus and go. Like Freddie and Basie would see that I had something to eat and a place to stay, so I never worried. Sometimes Joe would just say, "Well, I'm not working tonight. Kenny take my place." And I used to play with Basie all the time.
No kidding.
So Frank got this job at the Black Cat.
This was in the Village.

Yeah. And he told Lonnie Simmons, the bandleader, about me, so Lonnie hires me. So there was Freddie Green, Lonnie Simmons, Frank Clarke, Bobby Moore, who was the little trumpet player who played, "Out the Window," with Basie, remember?
Oh, yes.
That little trumpet player. He was working with us. So like we had trumpet, tenor, piano, bass and guitar. That was our band. And what a band that was.
And Lonnie Simmons was a friend of Freddie's from --
From South Carolina.
That's right.
They were raised together.
That's right.
And Freddie --
That's right, from Charleston or somewhere.
Well, wait a minute. Let's see --
No, not Savannah.
No. They're from South Carolina. I can't think of it.
It doesn't matter.
But I know it very well.
Yeah.

So what happend is that the rhythm section was so fantastic until everybody used to come and jam at the Black Cat. Benny Goodman, Harry James, Basie, Lionel, because I had vibraphones. And everyone used to come there and --
And this was practically your first job in New York.

Yeah, it was my first job really. My first decent job, you know. So everyone used to come and jam, and I'd look around -- the boss's name was Frankel, and Frankel used to keep Benny Goodman used to keep us there till 9:00 o'clock in the morning. And Harry used to come right by
the sock cymbal with his trumpet and blow into the sock cymbal.
(Laughter)
Which Harry?
Harry James.
For goodness' sake.
For heaven's sake.

Can you imagine? And Basie used to come all the time with Benny, you know, and jam with us. And that's when he got the idea, the way the rhythm section was jumping, he just took Freddie right out. I imagine if Joe hadn't been with the band I would probably have joined the band, too, you know.
Yeah.
Because the rhythm section was so perfect and I used to see a little crew cut guy in the audience, bobbing his head and weaving, and it was John Hammond.
(Laughter)
Every night. Just about every night. I think he was going to Columbia University at the time. And this little crew cut guy was jumping up and down.
(Laughter)
And later I found out it was John Hammond. In fact he paid the $54.00 to put us in the union, because it was a non-union house, the Black Cat, at that time.
No kidding. Well, did they have that -- didn't you have to go the six months to get in the union?
No, this was a non-union place.
Yeah, but then when you --
But the union was so happy to have the house in the union --
Oh, they just did the whole thing together. Oh, that was another break you've had.

So they were like telling me to join the union. I said, 'I don't want to join the union. I'm happy here, you know?' So John Hammond fixed it so I could join the union, and then the Black Cat came in too. So everybody was union so the Black Cat had to be union.
Yeah.
And Basie took Freddy away.
Yeah.
Well, at the time we were all leaving, because Lonnie, he wound up playing the Hammond organ in Chicago, he went to Chicago to do a single. Bobby Moore --
You mean he switched from tenor saxophone to --
To organ.
No kidding.
And you know, when the Hammond organ first became popular. First introduced. He was one of the first
ones to play the Hammond organ.
Was he really.
Yes, he was. Yes, he was.
I can remember Basie having that hankering to play the organ and being scared to play.
Remember?
Yeah.
Well anyway, I left to join the Blue Rhythm Band.
Lucky.
No, Edgar Hayes, with Joe Garland.
Oh.
That old Blue Rhythm Band. Remember?
Oh. It was with Mill's office, wasn't it?
Yeah. Yeah. Edgar Hayes. But we went on with Jimmy Lunceford, with Harold Oxley.
Well, he was a nice guy, Oxley.
Wasn't he? The only fair guy in the business. That's why he didn't stay.
Yeah.
He was beautiful. And they had Lunceford Enterprises, which took care of all the bookings.
[Walker]
And he handled T-Bone too, you know.
Oh, he did?
: Yes.
He was a beautiful man.
: He was a wonderful man, wasn't he.
Oh, I loved Harold Oxley. So fair.
: A really right person.
That's right. You don't find those kind of guys, never before or after, in the business.
: No, that's the truth.
Well, the formed the -- Harold Oxley and Jimmy Lunceford, they formed the Lunceford Enterprises.
: Yeah.
Then, after being with Edgar for -- I joined them in 1936, right after I left the Black Cat.
: Yeah.
Because I stayed there almost a year. And then, after Freddie left, then everybody became uneasy.
: Yeah.
And Frank, he joined Buddy Johnson's band.
: Oh, did he?
Uh-huh. And Bobby joined Basie and --
: Yeah. And Freddie had joined Basie.
Freddie joined Basie, and after, as Atkins, the a piano player, he went back to Philadelphia, and Lonny went to Chicago to play organ.
Funny, isn't it?
Isn't it?
(Unintelligible) -- and then all of a sudden everybody's all over the corners of the earth.
And I joined Edgar Hayes' band around the latter part of that year, and --
Well, tell me something about it. What was that band like?
It was the most fantastic band.
Was it?
That was the school. That was the university for me.
Was it?
That was it.
Was it?
Oh, yeah.
Well, tell me.
Well, Joe Garland -- well, I had started writing then, with Joe Garland and Rudy Powell and all those guys in the band. They just taught me --
Oh, that's where it all began.
They taught me everything.
No kidding.
And I used to write for the band, you know, like, you remember when the "Goona-Goon," tunes like that?
Yeah.
I used to make arrangements on that.
Yeah.
And I used to copy Ray McKinley.
You did?
Yeah, I used to copy him.
No kidding.
He was with Tommy Dorsey at the time.
Well, he had his own band.
Yeah, he did.
You know. And that was before he joined Tommy. Was it Tommy's band? But he had his own band.
Yeah.
But I used to buy all his records. I used to buy all his records.
Well, that's interesting.
Isn't that something? And I'd copy Ray McKinley.
No kidding. Does he know that?
No, I don't think he knows. That's when I first --
That might make him feel real good.
I never played -- I never was a soloist. I thought it was stupid. I always thought drum solos were very stupid, you know? So I never -- I always concentrated on

accompaniment. I thought that was the most important thing. That was my most basic function as a drummer, was to accompany, and so I always stuck with that. And I think that's why a lot of the musicians liked me so much, because I never show off and always think about them first. So, but Ray gave me the idea to play something, some kind of solo.
Yes.
So then I started copying his things and I started playing them, like little eight bar phrases and things like that.
Well, would you fit them in -- in the arrangement?
Yeah, I would have to.
Yeah.
I'd fit them. And then --
Well, I mean -- I want to know more about that. Would they come in behind somebody or would you make little holes in the arrangements and have it fit, or what?
Well, you know, that's when I started the style of playing along with the brass and making things like fill-in holes, as we call it, you know.
Yeah, like the bombs.
Yeah, with those little things. Started back as early as that.
Yeah. Because you were the first
guy that did it.

Yeah, but nobody understood it. They thought I was crazy. They said, 'Oh, that little guy is crazy. He's always breaking up the tempo.' So there it was. But I stuck to it. I thought I -- I liked it, so, you know, I wasn't about to change something that I had found, you know.
Yeah.
And I really had a flare with that.
So I stuck with it, on out.
-- End Side 3 --

Well, I want to talk to you more about that, and -- because it's kind of funny. You just got through saying that you didn't hold too much to drum solos and that you felt that you should be in back of a guy and supportive, and you know, and that was the thing.
Uh-huh.
And I mean I have to agree with you very much on that, because in this sense, that even today, in a way, the guys that feel for the band that they're working with --
Yeah.
-- and realize that guys look to -- that that is the foundation for them there. They're not out on their own. They've got to have that behind them.
Yeah.
And that's it. And the right drummer is relating to all the different guys in their own different
ways.
Right. Right.
: And giving him what he's needing.
What he's needing. That's right.
: Even if he doesn't really know what he's needing.
That's right. If you try to inspire him, you know, to --
: Yeah.
-- to -- like we used to say, kick him in the buns.
: Yeah.
You know, try to give him something to go on.
: That's right.
Give him a lift.
: That's right. That's right. Well, and of course, I mean, there always have been the drummers that didn't think like that.
No. No.
: And moreso -- the longer it went on the less the drummers think like that.
That's right. That's right.
: And the more they think about what they're doing up there, and making the show for themselves.
That's right.

Well, it's a strange -- it was really a new and strange development, that you went from that thinking and that feeling to what you might say like sounding off on the drums in a sense, because that's what you were doing really. You were creating a role for drums in the band.
That's right. That's right.
Not as a soloist, exactly, but like when you said you were working out like with the brass.
That's right.
You were fitting in with the sections.
Uh-huh.
Or creating another line along with the sections.

Right. Like when Joe Garland used to give me the trumpet parts, and he would say, 'Well, you play along with the brass where you think the emphasis is needed.' And so that way that gave me another dimension, you know, as far as reading and backing, you know, backing up brass, because I knew exactly what they were playing, because I saw it on the music, and then I would put what I thought was a good support for them, a special passage.
Yeah.
So all those things were just crowded in my mind.
Yeah.
That's why I say the Edgar Hayes Band was really my university.
Yeah. Yeah.
And a lot of the people, like -- well, Joe Garland wrote, 'In the Mood.'
Yeah.
Then Eddie Durham was writing for Glenn Miller.
Yeah.
So he asked me, 'Hey, Kenny, any new things? Because I'm writing. I need all the music I can get.' And I brought him, 'In the Mood.'
No kidding. No kidding. How about that.
So we --
Did Joe Garland get his on it?
Oh, he's still -- he made so much money from that. Oh, we had recorded it in 1936.
Yeah, I think I do remember that you had, a year or two before Glenn Miller did it.
Before, oh, yeah, about three or four years before Glenn Miller.
As much as that?
Yeah.
Well, did you -- when you started playing like this, did the whole brass section -- did everybody dig it?
Yeah.
They did?
Yes. The younger guys. And some of the older guys, they felt that because it kind of made what they were doing much more emphatic, you know?
Yeah.
You know?
Yeah.
Because they heard these things behind them and it gave such a lift to the band, you know?
But one thing it meant, I think -- I don't know -- but it meant that the drums had to be louder, because if they were -- in a sense, didn't it?
No, not louder, but sort of --
But coming in to spaces.
Another tone behind it, behind the brass, another color behind the brass.
Yeah. But would you say that it was an introduction to drumming that was louder? That it opened the field up for drumming that did become louder?
Yeah, that's more about the size of it, you know.
Yes.
Because I would try not to play too loud, not to drown out the brass.
No.
But to kind of give them the backing.
Yeah.
That I felt they needed. You know, by playing different passages with them, and then playing sort of like passages before we -- I mean to bring them into this passage.
Yeah, as a springboard.
Yeah, that's right.
Yes.
Sort of a springboard.
Yeah.
You know?
Yeah.
Because I knew exactly where they were going.
Yeah.
So I could kind of give them the right springboard they needed.
Well, you gave them a concept, a whole concept that was different, was new.
Well, yeah. When I started -- now, we
made this European trip with Edgar Hayes in December, '37. We went to Sweden and Finland. We did all the Scandinavian countries, Sweden, Finland, Norway --
Denmark?
Denmark. Then we came down to Holland and into Germany, Frankfurt, and then Holland, and then Belgium. Then we went back to Bremen, to go home.
Uh-huh. So we arrived home about May, '38.
That was a long tour.
It was a long haul, yeah. Fantastic tour.
Well, that was a new world. Well, let's not get -- let's hold up for a minute, because that's very interesting.
Okay.
But let's just talk, since we're right at this point, and since you are considered the father of modern drumming, or father isn't the word, really, it's like you broke the ground, you introduced it.
Uh-huh.
Well, let's just talk about drummers for a minute.
Well, Helen, how it really happened, I

had this idea in the back of my head ever since Edgar Hayes days, which the band gave me a chance to try all my possibilities, all the things that I thought I was capable of doing, and the things that I --
Explore.
Yeah, explore, exactly. So when I left Edgar Hayes, well then I went to Claude Hopkins, but I wound up with Teddy Hill and Dizzy, and that's where --
And that happened.
-- the whole thing happened.
Then it happened.
Because he understood being a man, rhythrical musician, Dizzy.
Yeah.
All kinds of rhythms fascinated him.
Yeah.
And so --
Latin rhythms, long when nobody was playing it.
Yeah. When Chano Pozo joined the band, that was.
Yeah.
Well, I used to write out little things, and Dizzy was right behind me, you know. I would write out a little thing and I would hand them back to him, you know. I'd

say, "Hey, Diz, how do you think this would sound?" He'd say, "Well, try it." So I began to play, you know, with my foot and left hand, and with the cymbal, because everyone says why don't you play the sock cymbal like this, and I say there has to be a better way, because if I play the sock cymbal then I can't use my left hand, you know?
Yeah.
So I have to find a way to use it.
So what did you do?
So I changed -- everyone wanted me to play like Joe Jones. But I didn't want to play like that.
No.
And I changed over to the top cymbal, which gave me the freedom of my left hand.
Yeah.
See, because Joe, he was cramped.
Yeah.

And I used to watch him. I used to follow Basie all over, to find out the advantage of playing the sock cymbal with the right hand like that, and I travelled all over the country with Basie, and sometimes would play in Joe's place, you know, to try to understand exactly --
Yeah.
But Joe, I don't know, I guess he had played that way so long that he had it quite undercover, exactly
what he wanted to do. But what he was doing had no bearing at all on what I wanted to do.
No.
I wanted to do something completely different.
Yeah.
And so I started playing this way, and freeing my left hand.
Yeah. So you became more ambidextrous.
That's right.
Yeah.
Because sometimes I would play and my idea was to never leave your left hand idle.
Yeah.

Because if people look up and they see me playing with one hand and this hand isn't doing anything, it's like a one handed piano player. So I said, well, I can't be one handed. I have to learn to play with this other hand.
Yeah.
So I began to work on it, to coordinate with my right foot.
Your left hand and your right foot?
And right foot. And my right hand with my left foot.
Gee.

You know, because rinky-dink, bang, I had the sock cymbal over here, and the left hand was the bass drum, so I figured, I said -- and I talked to Diz about it, and he said, "That's a perfect combination." Said, "Now you have the whole thing working." So then I began to work on it.
Well, so did you have drummers standing out there with their mouths open?

Oh, all the time. So Teddy Hill -- well, it wasn't his fault, it was some of the old trombone players, said, "Kenny keeps breaking up the time. Why doesn't he keep four beats on the bass drum?" So then I began to argue with them about the fact that if you are playing the tempo should be in your head, don't depend on me. Depend on yourself, because if you're playing music, the tempo that you're playing in is in your head. It's in your mind, or either it's no use of your being here, if you're depending on somebody to keep the tempo for you. You keep your tempo yourself. Because you can play the music without anything, alone. You can play your part.
Yeah, but you're asking more of them than --
That's what happened. So then they --
That's -- well you used to give them that framework, and they're not having it anymore.
No. So I was fired out of the band.
How long were you in the band?
Oh, let's see. We played the World's Fair with the band, too, in '39. So I was with the band about a year and a half. We did the whole 1939 World's Fair.
No kidding.
Then went to the Savoy Pavillon.
Yeah.
With Chick Webb.
Yeah.
And the Lindy Hoppers and all them.
Yeah.
We did the whole fair.
Down there at -- down the throughway and all that?
Yeah, the throughway.
Wasn't that called Freedomland?
Yeah. Almost at the end they had the Savoy Pavillion.
Yeah.
So we used to do 16 appearances a day.
And they had bands featured as well.
Yeah.
They had two places for bands.
Yeah, that's right.
Because I remember Benny Goodman
telling me he was down there.
So we were mostly featured with the Lindy Hoppers.
Yeah.
That was the big thing then.
Well, what did -- tell me something. Did you and Chick ever talk?
Oh, we played on the bandstand opposite each other.
With Edgar Hayes, or --
No, with Teddy Hill.
Oh.
Chick was on the left bandstand and we were on the right.
Yeah, that's right. That's right.
So every time, when we would finish, well I would be sitting behind Chick.
Well, Chick didn't -- he didn't -- he dug what you were doing, didn't he?

Oh, he always told me. He would come out to the fair and say, 'Kid, you're making great progress. You're doing fine, kid. Keep it up.' He would always encourage me. In the Savoy he said, 'Gee, what was that tune you just played?' You know? Although --
Oh, no, he was sincere.
I know he was, because I was --
Because he would say just the opposite if he meant it.
I was so close to him, you know, and why he liked me, God only knows. I guess, like I say, God has always been with me, all my life.
Well, the think about Chick was, I mean anybody that played he loved them. Whatever they played,
Yeah. I remember --
He was a guy that -- you know, music was everything to him.
That's right. That's right. That's what -- that was his life.
That was his life.
You know?
Well, tell me something, what kind of a drummer was he, then?
Oh, Chick -- I can't describe Chick.
Yeah. I know him so well. I want to hear what you think about it.
He was so fantastic, because I knew that I would never be able to play like Chick.
How come?
His conception. Not his technique and all.
No, no.
Because I could always copy his technique.
Sure. Sure, yeah.
But the way he played, I could never reach that stage. His conceptions, the way he would do things.
Throw himself in it. Project it.
Yeah. I could never do that. So --
Because that was his personality.
That was him. That was Chick.
Yeah.
And all I could do was enjoy it and try to get as much out of it as I could.
You got a thrill out of it.
Oh, my God, I would stay behind him all day, all night. All night long I was there. 'Hey, where's Kenny?' There I'd be, sitting behind Chick. That's where I was.
All right, let's go back a minute. Well, so at that time you were -- when Webb was playing the Savoy then and you were with Teddy Hill.
That's right. That's right.
Well, Roy was with Teddy, though, for a time.
Yeah. This was after. Because Roy had
just left the band, and --
And Diz had come in his place?
Diz, and then we had Al Killian.
Yeah.
And Joe Guy.
Yeah.
Those were the three trumpet players.
Yeah, I do remember that, yeah.
After Roy left.
Yeah, that's right.
And then --
Well, Joe Guy, I mean he had the same kind of ideas.
Yeah. Well, see --
Did Al Killian? I remember Al --
He wasn't much with solos. songs. He was kind of a Cat Anderson, you know.
Yeah, that's right.
At the time. He was the high note man.
Well, I remember he -- when T-bone was big on the West Coast, Al Killian made records with T-Bone then.
Uh-huh.
So I guess -- I guess, you know, he must have come out. Was he Texas or something?
I don't know. Maybe he was Texas. Maybe he was.
Yeah. I think that's what he was, yeah. Well, so -- but you say -- so it wasn't the brass section that, you know, felt that you weren't giving them the framework that you were used to.
No.
Who were the reeds?
Well, let me see. We changed quite a bit the reed section. We had Big Bob Carroll. You remember Bob Carroll?
Yeah.
And --
Wasn't he with Redman one time?
I think so.
Yeah.
He was with Don Redman.
That's what I said, Redman.
Yeah.
Yeah. That's right.
We had Bob and another tenor player named Hanpire (PHONETIC), Henry Hanpire. He was from Pittsburgh.
Oh. I don't know him.
And -- who was the alto player.
Well, it doesn't really matter.
I can't -- yeah.
It doesn't really matter.
But anyway --
Who was in that rhythm section with you? Who was the piano player?
That was -- who was the piano player? Wasn't it --
Weldon (PHONETIC)?
No.
Rodriguez? Or Dreyfuss (PHONETIC)?
No.
Where did Ram [Ramirez] come in?
I don't -- was it with Sonny White?
No.
No, it wasn't Sonny White. No. But the bass player was the old fellow who played. Oh, you know.
Yes, hard isn't it?
This old fellow.
Never mind. I'll remind you tomorrow.
I'll think about it.
We'll think.
But I can see his face just as clear.
Yeah. Well, anyway, that's -- we've really named the people in Teddy Hill's band who stood out.
Yeah.
Yeah.

Oh, Louis was the first modern musician.

So therefore he could understand, you
know, when he -- when he heard something that was akin to what he had been doing all his life, he recognized it immediately. So the guys in the band, we had, oh, like Prince Robinson and --

Yeah. All the old cats, you know. Well, Joe Garland, he was the musical director. Had Prince Robinson, and what was this other --
Had Luis Russell on piano.
Luis Russell on piano, and what's this saxophone player?
Oh, Cole?
That's right. That's right. What was his first name? Rupert.
Rupert.
Rupert Cole.

Ronnie.

Remember?

Well, Big Sidney was with the band. So he said, "Kenny, Pops digs you." Now, Pops had heard me play around with Louis Russell and all these bands, at the Apollo, because he was sweet on this little girl he married. She was a chorus girl at the Apollo Theater, so Louis used to be around a lot.

It is. It's extraordinary.
I just fall on my knees and pray all the time. You know? Which I've been doing since I was 12. But

Louis -- I mean Sid, he had been listening to me at Minton's, you know. He was the first one that put the word out. He said, "Man, that little cat is playing something out there. So he took me to the Renaissance Casino and set up his drums and brought the whole repertoire, Louis' whole repertoire, and we went through that book at least five or six times every day, for about four or five days. And he says, "Okay, I look, I'm going to join Benny," and he went to Detroit. And I joined Louis and we went to -- let's see, our first job was in Gary, Indiana. No, no, that wasn't the first one. He said, "Gizzard, where did you learn those?" I said, "I've just been listening." But I wouldn't tell him.
(Laughter)
I wouldn't tell him that Big Sid had took me over, because he would figure that there was a little conspiracy, you know.
Yeah, sure. How funny.
I said, "I've just been listening."
So he said, 'Doggone it, you play it like you've been playing it for years.' I said, 'Oh, thanks, Pops.' So we left there.
The guys must have been surprised, because when they hired you the guys must have been a little worried.
Well Joe, Joe Garland, you know, I worked with him with Edgar Hayes' band.
Yeah.
So he kind of backed it up and said, 'Yeah, Pops, that's the man,' you know, because he knew my work.
Yeah.

And well, we left Memphis and we played Gary, Indiana. That's the one that really cinched it, because he reached back in the book for things he thought I'd never heard before. But Sid took me through everything.
That's a really unbelievable story, isn't it?

And he reached back in the book and said, 'I'll get Little Gizzard. Play this.' And when we pulled out the music and I went right through it, and he said, 'Doggone, Gizzard.' And that was my man. Oh, it was wonderful.

Oh, we were just getting to be really --
What a shame. Oh, Neil Spencer didn't have such a big name anyway.

No, but he had been with Kirby, John Kirby and all that, you know. His name was much -- no-one knew who I was. They said, "That little kid who drops the bombs." That was about the biggest name I ever got. "That little kid who drops the bombs up at Minton's. You remember what's his name?"

So that was about the size of it.

Oh, now, that's disgusting.

And it was after the dance, which it was like a little town in Georgia, had no street lights. And there I was --
Why, that's a dangerous, awful thing to do.
And there I was in some town in Georgia. I don't know where.

Yeah, I was just a kid. And then, after the bus pulled out --
Well, how --
Well, it was on account of Joe Glazer and this road manager.
What a way of doing -- who was the road manager?
George Kroll his name was.
How disgusting. I know that Pops didn't ever stick his neck out on that kind of thing.
No, he wouldn't.
No.

Because I had my drums.
Yeah.
So he said, "Put your drums in the car,

kid. What are you doing out here? Let me get your out of here." So he took me to a colored restaurant, you know. And he said, "Are you hungry?" I said, "I have money." And entertain yourself. Yeah. Entertain yourself, and I'll come by and pick you up.

You've got a big guardian angel sitting on top of you.

We sat there and talked. We laughed and talked about all kinds of things, you know. He was telling me jokes, you know, about a 'possum running through the trees, and this and that, and we laughed. How amazing.

No. So I wound up in Liverpool and I began to play old church songs that I knew when I was a kid. I began to play for the --
Chaplain?

Yeah, for the priest. And I formed a quartet, and we used to sing, because I used to teach them every note and the harmony. So the priest heard this. He said, "My, this is wonderful, Kenny." So he kept me from going over on D-Day.
For goodness' sake.
I was in the marshalling area.
Oh, fancy that. There was your guardian angel again.

That's right. I was in [Tetworth] and all over. They put me right smack dab in the marshalling area where they were flying soldiers to the beachhead every day. So they called my name, and I said, "Oh, here we go. The landing." You know? So the priest says, "No, not Kenny, not him. I need him." So the Sergeant said, "Oh, okay. Okay. Okay. Okay."
You know, 'Okay, Father. Okay, Father.' So he said, 'Come, Kenny,' and he took me back to the chapel.
Fancy that.
And I didn't leave until -- I landed in Le Havre in the latter part of September.
And the landing would be June.
June 6th. And I went around the 14th of October.
Isn't that something.
Yeah. And I used to play -- you know, we had a foot organ.
Yeah.
You know, we'd pump air with our feet?
Yeah.
And I could play all those hymns I remembered, you know, and I would teach them to the guys in my outfit, you know. We formed a little quartet.
So, when you went over in October did he go along, the priest?
No, no, no. He stayed in England.
Oh.
He was at a very -- it was a very bad camp and we had a lot of incidents and things like that, so he stayed there and tried to keep order, you know. What was the name of that? Litchfield.
Oh.
And it got a very bad name, because they had the Colonel up for court martial, and a whole thing.
Had the Colonel up?
Yes, for court martial.
Well, what was he --

On account of prejudices and maltreatment of soldiers and all kinds of things. See, because the colored soldier, he wasn't allowed to go across the street. See, like the camp was bordered one side of a street, so on the other side of the street, they would tell the girls, the English girls, to walk over there.
Yeah.
And not near the camp.
Yeah.
But if a colored soldier crossed over he was shot dead.
You mean that happened?

Yes, that happened, at Litchfield. They had the Colonel up for court martial, and a whole lot of -- now, those were his orders, so the guys would try to sneak out under the fence and all that, you know. A lot of them -- oh, quite a few of them were killed. Guys in my outfit, you know. But the priest, he stayed to try to --
To try to make things a little better.
To make things a little better for the kids who stayed, you know.
Well, when you went over what was your company doing?
Well, I was in the smoke company, they called it. You know, camouflage.
Yeah.
I was trained in chemical warfare.
Yeah. So you didn't get into special services?
Yeah. Yeah, I got in after the -- you know, I went there as a smoke -- a chemical -- engineer.
Yeah. Part of the company that -- yeah.

But little by little I began to form little groups and they began to sing and then played in the church, and finally they made a company, the 13th Special Service, and I was head of the music department. And they elected a colored Lieutenant, Lieutenant Chaney (PHONETIC). So they put him over the company. So we formed the 13th Special Service right there.
For heaven's sake.
Uh-huh.
Well, that was good.
And I used to teach all -- I had 12 voices.
Kids who, you know, we picked out.
Yeah.
Kids who had at least a little talent.
Yeah.
We wouldn't pick out, you know, anyone.
No.
But the kids who really had voices, and I'd listen to them and think yeah, I want you, I want you. And we formed a chorale of 12 voices, and we toured, all up to the front lines and everywhere.
What would you sing?

Well, things like, 'Deep Purple,' 'Sleepy Lagoon,' a song that just came out -- what was that song. We used to play it at the Officers' Club and one of the Colonel's wives used to ask for it all the time. 'Sentimental Journey.'
Yeah.
Things like that.
Yeah.

And I would teach them every note, and they would remember, and I would wake them up in the morning and say, 'Now, let's go over it without the piano.' And they would -- I'd say, 'Do you remember your note?' He'd say, 'Yeah, Kenny, I've got it.' Because they knew they had to do it or either go over, you know.
Yeah.

So we -- I mean it was so wonderful, when we came to Paris we played at the Madeleine Theater, and there was a General Biddle who was chief of the Parisian area, who really hung down from the balcony and said, 'Great. Great, Sergeant. Wonderful work.' And Gertrude Stein and Alice B. Toklas were there, and they would say, 'How do you find time to do all this?' You know.
Fancy that. Isn't that amazing.
It was really wonderful
At the Madeleine Theater.
At the Madeleine Theatre, uh-huh.
Fancy that.
Uh-huh.
Well, then, did you get to the point where you got any guys who had instruments?
Yeah. We had -- I would pick out -- we had a pianist. I was playing trombone, and we had a --
They requisitioned a trombone?
Yeah. Well, we had all the instruments we wanted, you know.
Oh. Well, you hadn't played trombone in years, had you?
Yeah, well I played then. To keep from carrying the drums. I didn't want to carry the drums around.
Yeah.
So I taught another kid, in fact Mike, he's still playing drums in Detroit.
Fancy that.
And I taught him to play drums so that -- he was quite a big guy and he could carry the -- he could cope with the drums, you know?
Yeah.
So I couldn't cope with the drums and teaching everybody and directing the chorale, and all that, so --
So what other instruments did you have?
Well, we had an alto player, a pianist, a trumpet and trombone.
Oh, that's terrific.
And 12 voices.
How about that.
And bass. Yeah, we had a bass player, and he was a very good bass player.
And would you write stuff for these guys to play?
Yeah, for the instruments.
You'd write the music for the instruments?
But for the chorale, I had to teach every one, every note.
But by that time you knew you could write, couldn't you?
Oh, yes. I was writing from the age of 18. I was with a band, and --
Well, you didn't get any instruction on writing, did you?
No. I was telling you, this saxophone player taught me all my chords.
Yeah.
So he taught me -- when you're in a certain key on the piano, this is a certain key for the alto.
Yeah.
This is a certain key for the --
Oh, so you learned that.
So I learned that. So when I -- after I learned that, I just began to put two and two together and began to write, just like that, you know?
Did you ever -- I mean this is to digress a little bit, but did you ever actually write any arrangements for a full sized band?
Yeah, for Edgar Hayes' band.
You did?
I remember I did an arrangement on 'Goona Goo.'
Well, fancy that.
Yeah.
That's remarkable.
Well, all my life I've had to learn everything myself.
Yeah.
That's the story of my life.
That's how it is.
Yeah.
Well, listen, so when you were with this stage band in Paris would you get leave and be able to get out a little bit?
Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah.
So that was really your first introduction to Paris.
Yeah.
Wasn't it?
Yeah, that's right.
How long did that last, several months?
Oh,yeah. Let me see. Oh, we were -- we came -- we were stationed in Rouen, you know, in Normandy?
Yeah.

Where we made our landing. And we were guarding prisoners, German prisoners, there. We arrived in October, we stayed through Christmas. I remember because I remember German soldiers singing Christmas carols, and singing with our group along with them. And then it went up into the
Spring, till around -- you know, after the scare of the Battle of the Bulge and all that was over.
Yeah.
Because it happened that year. You know, in October, November and December of 1944.
Yeah.
So, after that scare was over we all went to the Ardennes to collect MIAs, you know, the Missing In Action, because we lost quite a number of soldiers.
Yes.
So we went in search of these soldiers.
Yes.
In the Ardennes Forest. Then I came back to France. You know, we did what we could do and found as many soldiers. You know, some of them were wounded and in private homes and all that kind of stuff.
Yeah.

So we came back to France and then they shipped us to Germany to a place called -- right outside of Heidelberg, it was a place we had to take a ferry across the river. Hasmesheim (PHONETIC). It's a little village called Hasmesheim. They gave me the job of taking in the morning report, every morning, which I had to go to Heidelberg every day with a jeep, you know. So that gave me a little time to air out things. And we left Hasmesheim and they sent me to Mannheim, and
there they put me in a unit to train the -- what do they call it? The GYA. What's it called? The German Youth Association.
Oh.
Which we had to show films, and sometimes we would teach music, and you know, try to get the German youth interested in things.
So this was like 1945.
Yeah.
Yeah, '45.
Yeah.
And --
Did you get any of the German language at all?
Oh, a little, you know.
Yeah.
I would just speak it when I had to.
Yeah, that's right.
When I didn't have to I didn't bother with it.
Yeah.
And there was a Captain who was assigned to our company whom I had went to school with in Pittsburgh, Captain Taylor, Arthur Taylor.
A black Captain.
Yeah. But I mean his mother was Danish.
Oh.
You know. He had big blue eyes and --
Fancy that.
But I knew his father. I knew his whole family, because we lived close together.
What an odd coincedence.
So he said to me one day -- I went to take a Major to Brussels.
Yeah.

So the Sergeant, when I -- I stayed about -- oh, I guess about 10 days, so when I returned, the Sergeant said, 'You're AWOL.' I said, 'What do you mean, AWOL? I was assigned to take the Major to Brussels.' He said, 'No, as far as I'm concerned you're AWOL, and you're going to be punished for it.' So he said, 'Captain, would you come out, please, sir? This AWOL has returned.' So the Captain walks out. He looks at me, he said, 'Kenny.' I said, 'Arthur.' So the Sergeant, he just dropped to his knees, because I was then -- so he said, 'What's wrong?' I said, 'This Sergeant's telling me I'm AWOL.' He said, 'Well, you took the --', 'When I arrived they told me you had taken a Major to Brussels.' I said, 'That's right, I did.' He said, 'Well, why is he AWOL.' The Sergeant didn't like me. Because we were musicians, you know.
Figured you were getting some privileges.

Yeah. So -- and then Arthur says to the Sergeant, he says, "Go get his dossier. Go get his papers. I want to see what Kenny -- Kenny, how long have you been here?" I said, "Too long, Arthur." You know. So he looked at it and he said, "Well, you have enough points to go home." So he sent me to a little town in Germany where I was supposed to take the train to catch the boat, and he sent me home.
Fancy that.

With all of my friends. He says, "Who do you want to go with you?" I says, "Well, him. Him." And we had Skeets Franklin, the bass player from Brooklyn -- yeah, he's from Brooklyn. And he was playing with us, so I said, "I want him, him, and --," and I took all my friends home with me.
What an extraordinary thing.
Isn't that something?
Isn't that? What an amazing thing.

So this Sergeant, he didn't know what to say. So he came over and started patting me and hugging me, and I said, "Don't hug me." You know. Because I know he wanted me to say a word for him to Captain Taylor, you know.
Yeah. What a funny -- and you didn't know that Taylor was there?
No, I didn't know because I had been away with the Major.
And he just got assigned.

He was just assigned while I was away, and when I returned, there he was, Captain Taylor. Oh, Captain Taylor. He said, 'Kenny, what are you doing here?' He says, 'You want to go home? Well, you have enough points. You have something like 57 points and you only need 55. Go home.'
And you might have been there a long time.
With that sergeant I would probably never have gotten out of the Army.
Yeah, fancy that. So he got you sent home, and how long did it take you to demob?

Well, while we were in Fort Dix I met James Moody, because they were all being demobilized also. Joe Gale, a tenor player. And we became buddies, you know. We would play around in the camp, because it took us about -- about 10 days to be demobilized.
Yeah.
So we were fooling around, and at the same time I had contacted Diz, you know, let him know, 'Well, Diz, I'm back, baby. I made it.' You know. So --
What happened to Diz, did Diz go, or what?
No, no. Diz was here with his band. He was in New York with his big band.
He never got called up then.
No. No. No. He was lucky.
He was lucky, wasn't he?

But we all showed. He told me, 'Well, Kenny, come to rehearsal at such and such a date.' He said, You'll get adjusted.' So I went home to see my brother and all that, and Carmen and I were married while I was in training.
I didn't know you were married to Carmen.
Yes.
I didn't know that.
Oh, she came down to the camp and we were married.
Well, how long had you know Carmen?
Oh, I'd know Carmen since the '30s, because she lived across the street from me, along with Charlie Holmes, Albert Nicholas. They all lived in the same apartment building.
Well, no wonder you and unintelligible were friends.
But I was --
Well, Carmen was going to school, was going to high school when I met her.

That's right, she was going to high school when I met her, too. She was going to high school when I met her. And Billy and I, we became staunch friends. So then Carmen and I, when I found out Carmen was a friend of Billie's, that was it, and with Irene. I was right in the crowd. I was one of the gang, you know.
Well, I never.
And I asked Carmen, you know, would she come down and see me, you know, because it was so lonesome. I said, 'Well, if you have time, would you come down, if you have time?'
(End of proceedings as recorded.)

You had just finished about you asked Carmen to come down and see you.
Yes, and she did, and we decided to be married while she was there.
No.
So I told her, 'Well, listen Carmen, I'm going away probably, overseas, and if --,'
Oh, you got married before you went overseas.
Yes. I said, well --
And I didn't even say that this was Carmen McRae we were talking about, did I?
No.
No.
So I told her, 'Well, since I have really no family, and they pay wives a certain amount of money for soldiers who are going overseas --,'
That's right.
'So I would like for you to have it.'
That's right.
'Because you're my best friend.'
Yeah.
'And I would like for you to have that.'
