Yeah, before you go.
And we were married there in Gadsden, Alabama, in Etowah (PHONETIC) County.
(Laughter)
For goodness' sake.
And all the fellows in the band came down to witness for me and everything like that.
Fancy that. Well, that's tremendous. Well, then, so when you got back then, was Carmen -- Carmen was -- I guess she was on the road, was she? Or, she was home?
No, she was home. She was home.
She was home?
Yeah, she was.
Well, that was wonderful, wasn't it?
Yeah.
So -- well, what happened then? So you got in touch with Dizzy.
Yeah. Well, I showed up at rehearsal, as I was telling you, when I came home, and at rehearsal I looked at the fellows in the band, and there sat James Moody and Joe Gales.
Oh, for heaven's sake. They --
Yeah, Dizzy had contacted them some way or other.
Isn't that funny.
And there he sat in the band. And I was so amazed. And you know how Moody...
How extraordinary.

So during this rehearsal -- well, we had several rehearsals, but during one of the rehearsals, I was just about to leave home, 'cause I lived up near City College, just a couple of doors from there, on Convent Avenue. So I get a telephone call just before I'm about to leave, you know, and it's John Lewis, who'd arrived from Albuquerque, and he said, "Listen, Kenny, I told you I would meet you in New York." I said, "Well, I'll be darned. What are you going to do?" He said, "Well, I'm supposed to go to Columbia," because he has a degree in anthropology from the University of New Mexico.
Yes.
Et cetera, et cetera. And he was supposed to come to Columbia to study music, I suppose.
Yeah.

And I said, "Well --," I had told him while we were in the Army that I knew Dizzy Gillespie, so everyone laughed and said it was Army tales, and so forth. So I don't know whether he called me just to see if I knew Dizzy or whether he called me to let me know that he was here, and --
But you didn't tell me where you met John Lewis.
In the Army, here in France.
When?
Well, in 1944.
Well, what was he doing?
Well, he was in the -- this colored division, what was it -- 92nd Division.
Yes.
They had been to Italy.
Yeah.
And they came back to France, a great part of them, you know.
Yeah.
And I was assigned to their company, to that outfit -- division, rather.
Oh.
And there I met John Lewis, who had formed a band and all that in the 92nd Division.
Oh.
It was remnants of the 92nd Division.
Yeah. Yeah.
So most of the guys were from Chicago, you know.
Yeah.
So there I met John Lewis, and we began to play, and rehearse, and have fun playing music. So I was -- I used to tell him, you know, I knew Dizzy Gillespie and Billy

Eckstine, and everybody would laugh. So when John came to New York, I said, "That's fine. That works out just great, because I'm on my way to rehearsal. Why don't you pass by and pick me up, and I'll give you my address and we'll go together." So he shows up and we go. I said, "Bring that music we used to play when we were in the Army." Because we used to play, "Two Bass Base Hit," but we called it, "Bright Lights," while we were in the Army. So he brought his music along and we went along to rehearsal. So we were rehearsing awhile, so I asked Diz, I said, "Hey, Diz, there's a young guy out there who served with me in the Army." I said, "He's a wonderful arranger and a wonderful pianist and a great guy," you know. So Dizzy says, "Oh, yeah? Where is he, man?" I said, "There, he sits right there." So I said, "He brought along some of his music." He said, "Yeah?" I said, "Yeah." So I went and got John, and I said, "Give me 'Bright Lights,'" because I knew that was a hit. That was a tune that everyone loved in the Army. So I said, "Give me 'Bright Lights'." So he came with the music, and Dizzy said, "Pass it out, Kenny." So I passed the music out, and we got through the introduction and to the first chords, and he looked at John, he stopped the band, and he says, "You want to work with us?" So John, you know, he was timid, and he said, "Well, yeah, you know." So Dizzy said, "You're hired." We hadn't even finished the arrangement. Dizzy heard right away the talent that this man had.
Yeah.
And we hired him right on the spot.
How about that.
And then --
Was Dizzy using a piano player then?
Yeah. We had -- let's see.
So John was paid to write.
Yeah, to write. He was on the arranging staff.
Yeah.
Which was John Lewis, Walter Fuller and Dizzy. We had three arrangers.
Yeah.
So --
Is that the saxophone player, Walter Fuller?
No. No. No, he's an arranger.
Oh.
Strictly an arranger. He doesn't play any instruments.
Yeah.

So, well, we worked around a little bit, you know, and John was coming along with the band. Sometimes he would stay in New York and so forth. So one day we played the Apollo Theater. So Monk and I went to the Braddock Bar to

have a drink during the half hour, you know. So we were there, drinking beer and talking and laughing. So I looked at my watch, I said, "Oh, my God, Monk, we missed the half hour." And he said, "Oh, oh." So some way I said, "We better get out of here." He said, "Yeah, we better." So we ran backstage and there was Milt Jackson, sitting up on the drums, but behind the curtain I sneaked up under the curtain and sneaked up on the stand, I said, "Bags, hey Bags." So Bags, he said, "Is that you, Klook Klunk?" I said, "Yeah. Let me get up. Let me get up." He said, "Okay, okay." So he gave me the sticks and I climbed up on the drums and Bags climbed down, and when Diz looked up, there I was, playing. So he looked at me and said -- so I just kept playing. "Yeah, man, here we go." You know. So Monk walked in behind me to the piano. So before he could sit down, he was coming through the wings -- before he could sit down, Dizzy looked at him and pointed. He said, "And you, you're fired." But he fined me $25.00, which Lorraine said, "No, give Kenny his money. No, don't do that." "Because he was there playing and he did not miss the show. All he missed was the theme song."
Lorraine's nice like that.

Yeah. She said, "Give Kenny his money." $28.00 he fined me. But Monk, he said, "You're fired." So John Lewis was sitting in the wings, and so Dizzy just beckoned, he said, "John." And John came to play the --
Diz was real mad, then.

Oh, he was mad with Monk, because Monk, he comes in like he missed the whole thing. I don't know why he was waiting out there. Because no-one was at the piano, so he could have sneaked in easily, more easily than I did, you know. But he just stood in the wings, wanted to be grand, you know, and Dizzy just pointed and said, "You're fired." And John Lewis came right in and sat down with the piano, and there it was. He was the pianist from then on.
Fancy that.
And Monk was our pianist.
So this was how John's career got launched.

Uh-huh. And John, he used to want to do something for me, you know. He said, "What can I do?" I said nothing, nothing. He said, "Do you need money?" I said, "No, I don't need a thing." You know? Everything is beautiful.
That was nice.
He couldn't get over it, you know.
Yeah.
When I said, "Well, it's your talent, you know."
Yeah.
I just happened to find a place to place
it, you know. So make the best of it you can.
Yeah.
So then he never looked back. He just kept going on.
That was wonderful.
Which is beautiful.
Yeah.
And as far as the Modern Jazz Quartet, we formed it.
Yeah. That's what comes next, doesn't it?
Yeah.
Well, wait a minute. I don't know that it does. Hold on a second.
No, we came to Europe with Diz.
Yeah, that's right.
Yeah.
Yeah.
So I had left the band, you know, when they just -- I stayed with the band to '46, and then I left.
You went with Tadd Dameron, didn't you?
Yeah. This was after Diz. See, I left Diz's band in -- well, I hadn't been there quite a year.
Why'd you leave him?
I don't know. I don't know. Just something.
Something, yeah.
Something came up. I wasn't mad with Diz or nothing like that.
No.
It was just something I wanted to do.
Yeah.
You know.
Right.
So I left Diz, but John stayed with the band, you know, he kept right along, and the band was going good. So I joined Tadd.
Yeah.
Because Tadd had this job at the Royal Roost.
Yeah.
And like we were there, you know, we could stay there as long as we wanted to.
Who all was it?
Oh, we had -- we changed the band quite a bit. We had like Fats Navarro, Wardell Gray, Allen Eager, Dexter Gordon.
Good gracious.
Miles Davis. We just about had all the
My goodness.

And -- well, we became the house band. So we began to record quite a bit. Tadd was very popular at that time. And he was writing for Dizzy, you know, things like -- we recorded quite a few of Tadd's things, you know, with Diz's band.
Oh, yeah.
Like, 'Our Delight,' and 'Stay On It,' things like that, you know.
Yeah.
So Tadd was kind of attached to Diz, which we were all attached to Dizzy.
Yeah.
Because Dizzy was the high priest.
Yeah.
You know.
Yeah.

And one day -- well, they had Joe Harris was playing with the band, Diz's band, at the time. And something that Joe was doing that wasn't comfortable for Dizzy, you know, the rhythm section wasn't comfortable.
Yeah.
So he asked me would I make the trip to Europe with him.
Yeah.
And I said, 'Oh, Diz, I can't do that. I'm with Tadd, and we have our little thing going, you know.'
Yeah.

Which was -- we had Ernie Henry. Oh, we had a good group. We would change, you know, frequently. And I said, 'Oh, no, man, Diz, I can't make it.' So he said, 'Oh, don't be a drag, Klook, come on. Come on.' I said, 'No. I'm happy with Tadd, Diz, and you do your thing, and we're still boys. We'll always be friends, you know, as long as I live. But I don't -- I'm not in the mood to go to Europe. I just left Europe in the Army.'
Yeah.
'And I have some --,'
You were home at last.
Yeah. I wanted to stay home with my wife and all.
Yeah.

So he said, 'Okay, but you're still a drag.' So he goes and gets Lorraine and brings Lorraine down the next night. So Lorraine says, 'Kenny, I'd like to talk to you.' So in the back of my mind I was thinking -- because you know, I love Lorraine, you know. So Lorraine says, 'Now, listen Kenny, we need you to make this trip. It's very important. It's going to be a very important trip, and we would like for you to
make it." Then I began to think, you know. I said, "Now, what is this." You know. So before the night was over I told her okay, I'll go.
(Laughter)
No fool, Dizzy.
No.
(Laughter)

MR. CLARKE: Diz, you know, he looked at me with that sly look, said, I got you, I knew I'd get you. So then we went to the Savoy Ballroom, with Chano Pozo and all that, and we formed -- I think it was the greatest band Diz ever had. And we made this famous trip to Europe with Chano Pozo and all. But what really happened on this trip, this trip, it made me realize that I didn't belong in the States. Well, what happened, this fellow, a Swedish fellow, who organized the tour, I had known him from 10 years before, in 1938. So we had travelled Third Class in 1938, which was my first trip. I was happy to be in steerage or anywhere, you know. But when we went to the pier and took the boat, and they assigned us to our cabins, then I saw a steward whom I had known 10 years before, Hans. We were riding on a Swedish ship, on the [Drottningholm.] So I -- and Lundquist had told me. He said, "This time, Kenny, it's in the contract. Everything first class from here out." He said, "It won't be like in '38. Everything first class." So I said, "Oh, Lundquist, that's beautiful." He said, "Dont't worry, this is

going to be really something," you know. So when we get on the ship, I see the Steward, and I said, "Hey, Hans, how are you?" He said, "Okay." And we hugged and everything. I said, "You're up in first class now." He said, "No, I'm still in third." I said, "You mean we're in third class." He said, "Yeah." So I asked Dizzy, I said, "Hey, Diz, man, you better look at your contract." So then all the other musicians began to follow me. They said, well, something's wrong because Kenny's up in the air and frothing at the mouth. Something's wrong, you know, so let's find out. They were following me around and peeping and listening. So Lorraine was in the cabin, so I said, "Listen, Diz, Lundquist told me that everything is first class." I said, "What are we doing here in third?" So Lorraine said, "Yeah, Diz, you'd better get that contract out and look at it." "Because," I said, "I know we're in third, because there's a Steward, Hans, I've known him for 10 years, and he can tell you we're in third." So he looked at the contract and it said first class. So what the Shaw office had done, they had raked off the top of the first class money and put us in third, because they figured, well, they don't know the difference.
No.
Yes, sir. Then, after we straightened it out, and we made them pay us the difference of the third class -- now, I 'm the instigator of all this, because I couldn't stand it.
No.
When something's wrong, it's wrong.
Yes. Absolutely.
So we made them pay us the difference of first class. We said, 'Okay, we're assigned to our cabins, but we want that money, the difference.'
Before you even sailed?
No, we got it on our way back.
Yeah.
Then, Lundquist had -- we had talked, because we were old friends from the trip with Edgar, you know?
Yeah.

And we had talked. He'd said, 'You won't have to work these days and you get paid extra for this.' So they had told us, 'Well, you get a flat salary, so much a week.' So I said, 'No, no, no, no.' I said, 'Look, Lorraine, let's go over it again, the contract.' So we read over the contract again and we found out we were supposed to get extra money for certain days, for so many days a week extra money, so it cost them something like a little over $20,000.00, that they had taken. Well, the son of Billy Shaw, Milt, was telling me, he says, 'Well --,' before all this happened, you know, before I saw -- had seen Hans, you know. He said, 'Well, I'm going to buy a nice new Oldsmobile when we get back, and you're going to be the first one I'm going to ride. You're going to be
the first one to ride in it." So I said, "Oh, yeah, nice, you know, nice." I hadn't dreamed that it was our money he was going to buy the Oldsmobile with.
No.

So after all this came up, all these things, so we arrived in Sweden, and his father made him come back. He was supposed to travel with us. All this 20,000, or $27,000.00, I forget exactly how much money, but I know it was a large sum of money, he was supposed to travel with the band and all. So when we arrived in Göteborg, we came off on a tender. We put all the instruments on the tender, you know, because the boat was like a mile out, you know.
Yeah.
So we had a concert that night, so we came in on a tender.
Yeah.
So we couldn't go through all the passport regulations.
Yeah.

So they rode us in on the tender. So while we were riding in I was standing on the edge of the boat, looking over at the sea, you know, admiring it. You know, it's like a return to something I had known 10 years before, and I was enjoying.
Yeah.

And Milt tried to push me off of the boat. And Al McKibben was sitting like -- you know, I was standing here, and like this was the rail of the boat, so Al was sitting inside like this, you know, beside me. Because we had been talking. I was saying, "I remember this, and I remember this." So he runs up to push me, and Al says, "Look out, Kenny," and he grabbed him. I said, "What are you trying to do, man? Are you crazy." So he looked at me and said, "I'll kill you." So Al McKibben said, "No, you won't, either. You must be crazy, are you kidding?" So then his father sent for him to go back, because he was mad because I had exposed this whole thing. He was very angry about it. So then Lorraine, I told Lorraine, I said, "Look, Lorraine. You need those people like a hole in the head." So Lorraine became Dizzy's manager. I said, "All you have to do is go to the union and pay $5.00 and you become a manager." And she said, "That's what I'm going to do." And she's been managing Dizzy ever since, and Dizzy never made so much money in his life.
Because they were taking it.

They were stealing it from him. So Lorraine said, "They won't steal any more, because I'm going to manage it from now on out," you know. So that's why we're real tight. Lorraine, she is -- I love her, because she got the message immediately. She says, "Oh, they won't rob Dizzy, not while I'm alive." And she manages his affairs right till
now. She -- sometimes I go there and she's in paper work up to there.
Yeah, I believe it.
But she takes care of all his business, answers his letters, makes the prices, does everything. Can you imagine that?
And that's what it springs from.

You see? Now, then, they told me, he says, "That's all right. You'll never work in New York again." So I began to calculate, I said, "Oh, yeah, I guess I'm washed up there." It's still going on today. Because George Wein, I knew him when he was in school, in high school, because his brother -- I worked at a club, his brother was manager, at the [Kitten] Club in Boston, and George, he was about 15 or 16 years old, was still going to high school. But the message got out about Kenny is a troublemaker. So Norman Granz, George Wein, those people, they never hire me, never. But you know, I just laugh at them, you know, because I say, "I need you guys like a hole in the head." If you fellows are paying the slave wages you're paying in America, I can't use it." So to give you an idea, when I was in the States last year, I worked in Chicago with Al Haig, and the boss and I, we talked it over, and he says, "Look, Kenny, I can only give you 250 a night." I said, "Well, don't worry about it." I said, "Well, I'm going to be here anyway, so it's okay." So I finished the job there

at the Showcase and come to New York. So Joe Newman's wife [Rigmor] was running the place for Joe. [Storyville] So you know what they offered me? $50.00 a night. I said no. She said, "Well, everybody gets $50.00 a night." So then was when I learned that it was George Wein owned the place. The Storyville, or whatever it is. $50.00. That's what they offered Kenny, $50.00. She said, "Well, everybody gets $50.00." I said, "Not me." I said, "I wouldn't go around the corner for $50.00, and I've been in Paris 20 years and I've never worked for that kind of money since I've been over there, so I'm not coming back home to work for $50.00 a night." So he sees me in New York -- in Paris, at the Palais de Chaillot, he says, "Well, when you come to New York I'll give you a job." I said, "I don't want a job. I don't need a job. And please don't offer me a job." So that was the end of that. So they never offered me anything. So I'm glad about it, because I --
Well, whatever -- I mean you're so right. Anything they do, it's done just that way.
Yeah, it happened. That's how it all happened, you know. But I just couldn't stand to see Dizzy taken like that, you know. As tight as we were.
Yeah.
As good friends as we were, I couldn't, no. I said I'll die first, but I'm sure going to tell Dizzy what's happening.
Yeah.
And I did. So that kind of washed me up for New York. So, luckily, I came to Paris and I stayed, you know.
Well --
After the band finished working, I stayed on, you know.
Oh, yeah.
And John, he went to study with a pianist, Madame Proto, to study piano. So he stayed over with me, you know.
That was in about '48.
'48, uh-huh.
Yeah.

So I stayed, from where we finished our work in February, and the band went back, so Dizzy said, 'You're not coming?' I said, 'No, I'm not going back. I'm not going back to hell again, you know, with all those agents down my throat.' So I stayed over and Dizzy took my drums back. And John and I, we left in August, in August of '48. So I stayed all winter in New York.
All winter in Paris.
No, in New York. I left Paris in August.
Oh, I see, yeah.
I stayed in New York all winter, and that

spring, Madame Nicole Barclay, who owned the Barclay Record Company here, she came to New York to form a group to play the First Paris Festival. So she said right away, "I want Kenny Clarke first." Now, you'll get whoever else you want, but Kenny Clarke is first." Now, this was what she told the agents, so they were up in the air. They didn't know what to do. So she said, "Now, I want him, first. Otherwise, you forget it. I'll get him to pick the musicians." Which would have meant it would have cut off their percentage. So they shopped around and got Miles, Tadd, they got all the people that I liked, you know. They were trying to make me happy, because they knew that I was going to lead this whole thing. I had spurned the whole thing. So they got Moody, Tadd, Miles, Barney Spielman bass, and myself. Five pieces. And they got Bird, Max, Al Haig, all my friends. You see how it works out? Because if they had chosen someone against my wishes, then I would have said, "No, Nicole, we don't take him." So they tried to find every one who they thought I would approve of.
Yeah.
And there was Bird, Max, Al Haig, Tommy Potter.
Oh, Max. Well, you were going to be playing drums, weren't you?
No, it was a festival.
Oh, I see, yeah.
It was the First Paris Festival.
: I see, yeah.
So we were picking out the musicians to make this festival.
: Yes, I see.
Then Tommy Potter, Al -- (End of Side 9)
: So we were just saying that that was broadcast.
Uh-huh.

Yeah, they just bought the tape and I just received the money from the union, so I know.
(Laughter)
: Yeah.
That the record will be out.
: Fancy that.
And like I said, it's -- well, it's been 28 years, almost 30 years ago, and now they decided that that was a very good broadcast. It was a fantastic festival.
: I wouldn't even have thought of that.
Well, this new -- well, it's between two people. Now, there's the Paris representatives of Columbia,
he's a pianist.

And a very good friend of mine. So like he looks into things and finds out what is really worthwhile.

Is he really.

Now, we just did this this Sunday past, you know.
Is Bert -- Blumenthal?
Uh-huh.
Yeah. Oh, that's splendid, isn't it?
So now Henri's going to push it, because --
What's -- how do you spell his last name?
R-e-n-o-u-d.
Oh, Renaud.
Uh-huh. Renaud.
I see.
So he's going to push it and --
Very good. Very good. Well, okay.
So well now, we haven't got all the time in the world, so I've got to get you from that festival --
Uh-huh.
-- you came -- you know, one of the things is I've got a note here that says after the end of the tour with Dizzy that you did some recording and teaching in Paris. Did you?
Oh, yes, I did. Yes, I did.
You got a taste for that, too.
Yeah.
Yes.
We did quite a few things with John, with Cecil Payne, and we put the -- I took those tapes home and we put those tapes out on the DG label, the Dizzy Gillespie label.
Really?
Uh-huh. Which they weren't exploited to the nth degree, you know.
Well, they didn't have distribution.
No, no, because there was a friend of Dizzy's named Dave Usher, from Detroit, who was taking care of the distribution, which he didn't know very well.
Yeah.
The record business was new to him, you know.
Yeah. It's tough, isn't it?
Yeah.
Well then, so did you go back to the Royal Roost with Tadd then?
No, no. No, I stayed over here from that festival on. I stayed two years. I stayed till '51.
Oh. I see.
Uh-huh.
So -- oh, I see.
I went home in May, '51.
Yeah.
Uh-huh.
I see.

And just -- I got off the boat, and went straight to the studio. Someone was -- I met someone who was telling me that Diz is recording. So he was recording at that time, "The Champ," with Art Blakey, and I walked right in the studio and everybody fell out. "You mean you're back?"
(Laughter)
How funny.
So that was in '51, May, '51. Then, during the five years I stayed home.
Yeah.
And I started out with -- well, I worked with Stan Getz, with Duke Jordan and Bill Crow on bass. Then I went back to Minton's.
Oh?
You know? And Teddy says, 'It's your joint. Do what you want.' So then we formed an MJQ, but it was the Milt Jackson Quartet.
Oh. Really?
And we had --
When had you got to know Milt? Bags.
Well, I knew Bags right after the war.
Yeah.
He came to New York. Well, Diz had brought him to New York.
Oh.
Along with Ray Brown.
Yeah.
All these young kids.
Yeah.
And Joe Harris, the drummer, you know.
Yeah.
So I met them all on 52nd Street.
Yeah.
Because we were working at the Spotlight
with Dizzy's big band.
I see.
You know? So that's when I met Milt.
So then --
So then we recorded --
Up there at Minton's you formed the --
Yeah, formed the Milt Jackson Quartet, with Percy Heath --
John.
No. No, John was going to the Manhattan School at the time.
Oh, yeah.
You know, after the band broke up, he went to -- back to school.
Back to school.
And so we had -- oh, we had Gildo Mahonas (PHONETIC), whatever his name is, on piano. Then we had Horace Silver.
You did?
Oh, yeah. Well, we made the first Newport Jazz Festival, was the MJQ with Horace Silver on piano.
Oh, really?
Uh-huh.
Fancy that.
And, well --
So you and Horace and Percy and Milt.
And Bags, yeah. Yeah, that was the quartet. Then when I went to Minton's we hired Sonny Rollins. So I got -- Sonny was hanging around, not doing much.
Yeah.
So I got Teddy to hire Sonny.
Well, the quartet didn't have that character that it got afterwards.
No, no.
It didn't have that subdued character.
No, no. It was just straight out swing.
Yeah.
Having a ball, you know.
Yeah.
So then we got Sonny Rollins, which we did a lot of recordings with Sonny, and we recorded quite a bit with another alto player, who was --
Sonny --
No. No. He was with -- he had the contract with Blue Note. So we began to record with him a lot.
Can't you get that name?
It's right on the end of my tongue, like always.
Who was he working with before?
Oh, he was just a kind of a --
He was just coming up.
Yeah, just coming up, but very good, a very good alto player. Oh, we did a lot of records with him. I can't think of his name.
That wasn't Lucky Thompson, was it?
Oh, no. No, no. No, no. No, he was an alto player, a good alto player, too. Oh, why can't I think of his name?
Well, never mind. It'll come.

Then, this was around '52, '51, the latter part of '51, as I started right into working, you know, trying to get things done as quickly as I could. And well, we did quite a few things, you know, at Town Hall, with J.J., and things like that.
Yeah.
But we'd always stick together.
Yeah.
And we got so tight together that Percy and I, any tune you'd call, we could start off playing without stomping off. We just knew all the tempos.
No kidding.
And we had such an understanding, it was fantastic.
Yeah.
Really fantastic. And, well, we went to work in the Blue Note in Philadelphia, and then I went to work with Oscar after that.
You did.
No, this was after I left the Modern Jazz Quartet. But we went to, with the Modern Jazz Quartet, after John left school, then we -- John came with us, and from there we started this John Lewis --
Approach.
Approach to jazz.
Didn't you go for that?
No, not at all. Because like he would say sometimes on things, like, 'Kenny, this isn't supposed to swing.' I said, 'What is it supposed to do?'
(Laughter)
So this went on. We did -- we really formed the Modern Jazz Quartet in Birdland. That's when we really started playing together.
Yeah.
Then we played a little club on -- where was it? It was called the Staircase or something like that.
Yeah.
And we stayed there for awhile. Then we went on tour, went to Birdland, then we went on tour with Sarah Vaughan, Count Basie, because we were in --
Oh, a package deal.

Yeah, a package deal. We were in Birdland with Count Basie. So we left Birdland and we went on tour with Basie and Sarah and all that. Then we got a deal to go to San Francisco, at the Black Hawk, and that did it. One of the famous photographers -- what was his name? He was fantastic. One of the most famous at that time. Well, anyway, he took pictures of us and put us in the leading paper in San Francisco.
Yeah.

And the dowager of San Francisco society came out for us. She said, 'They are the most marvelous musicians.' So that did it. And she says, 'They are playing 18th Century drawing room music and swinging.' So that was all we needed.
Yeah, something new.
Yeah. So then Ralph --
Gleason.
Ralph Gleason, he would just spread us all over. So when we came back to New York we had quite a name for ourselves.
Oh, yeah.
You know.
Yeah, well you were the biggest thing around then.
Yeah, that's right. That's right.
When you really broke you were the biggest thing.
And we came back to New York and went back to --
And that was co-op, wasn't it?
Huh?
You guys were splitting that, weren't you?
Yeah. So --
That was good money, then.
Oh, yeah. Yeah, it was good then.
Yeah.

And we came back to New York, around '54 now, and John says, well we have a new member. I was thinking what instrument did he play to add anything, to complement Milt, what instrument could that be. No. Not equal.
No manager, no. Not equal. Because he's sitting down.
Yeah.
And answering telephones, and we're out there on the road.
Yeah.
Scuffling. Plus, we're playing.
That's right.

You know? So I said no, that's no deal, John. I don't think -- that's not right. So now, see, Milt and Percy didn't open their mouths. It was only me talking. So, John Lewis was giving piano lessons to one of John Hammond's daughters or sons, I don't know, one of his children. Anyway, he must have explained to John Hammond what was going on. So I felt John brought it up and said, 'Get rid of him.' So when they came to work that night I felt something strange, you know. So Bags said, 'Don't leave, Klook. Don't leave.' So, well, I don't know, you know, what's going on. So they were leaving for Washington, the Howard Theater. So I went home that night and thought about it. So when they arrived in Washington I didn't show up. I went out to Carmen's mother's house and went to sleep. I decided not to go. You know. Because if he would let someone foreign, someone who had nothing to do with us, kick me out. Monte, he would say, 'See, like all the agents say, Kenny Clarke's a trouble maker, you know?' And I felt it right away, you know.
Uh-huh.
So I decided well, I won't cause him any trouble. I'll just get out.
How sad, with what you'd done for John.

That's right. He went for that, and that's what made me so -- I was like -- I couldn't believe it. I said, "No, this is not possible." But that's the way it was. So I saw Milt there, you know, was it the month of -- June, he was here. So he says, "After 20 years I finally got out of there." He says, "The only thing I have against you is you didn't take me when you left."
(Laughter)

You know? Because Monte wound up stealing their money, like I knew he would, and Bags said, "I wonder if something's funny." He said, "After we broke up we started making $5,000.00 a concert." You know, before something drastic happens and you really lose friendship with people.
Yeah.
So before that all comes, while he still speaks and hugs me and kisses me and all that John does, you know, but I feel back in my head that it's not kosher.
No.

Yeah. Well, as a matter of fact, Kenny, you'd have never kept it up anyway, would you?
No. I couldn't. No, no, not 20 years.
No.
My God, no.
No.

-- I began to work with Phineas Newborn, Oscar and I, you know.
